summary.text: Decomposing factorials into their powers of \(p\) and unit blocks, then pairing units \(u\) and \(-u\) modulo \(p^r\), yields a relative \(p^{3r}\)-congruence for \(C_m(k)=(mk)!/(k!)^m\). A Dwork-style exponential integrality criterion identifies the recursive coefficients with the formal exponential; splitting its logarithm into indices divisible and not divisible by \(p^r\), together with a carry-count valuation bound, gives the desired coefficient congruence for \(m\ge2\), while \(m=1\) reduces to half a central binomial coefficient and the same factorial-ratio congruence.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 C_m(k):=\frac{(mk)!}{(k!)^m}\qquad(m,k\geq 0).
\]
This is an integer: it is the multinomial coefficient obtained by dividing a set of size \(mk\) into \(m\) ordered blocks of size \(k\). Put
\[
 A_m(x)=\exp\left(\sum_{k\geq1}C_m(k)\frac{x^k}{k}\right).
\]
We shall prove that every coefficient of \(A_m(x)^n\) is an integer and, for \(m,n,r\geq1\) and every prime \(p\geq5\),
\[
 [x^{np^r}]A_m(x)^{np^r}\equiv [x^{np^{r-1}}]A_m(x)^{np^{r-1}}\pmod {p^{3r}}.
\]
This is precisely the assertion about \(b_m\).

Throughout the proof, \(v_p\) denotes the usual \(p\)-adic valuation on nonzero rational numbers, with the convention that a statement \(v_p(0)\geq a\) is always true. Thus saying that a rational number is divisible by \(p^a\) means that its valuation is at least \(a\); the exponent \(a\) is allowed to be an integer. We repeatedly use the elementary facts
\[
 v_p(xy)=v_p(x)+v_p(y),\qquad
 v_p(x+y)\geq\min(v_p(x),v_p(y)).
\]

## 1. A factorial-ratio supercongruence

The principal arithmetic input is
\[
 v_p\bigl(C_m(pn)-C_m(n)\bigr)
 \geq 3r+v_p(C_m(n))                         \tag{1}
\]
whenever \(r>0\) and \(p^r\mid pn\). We first prove this.

For a positive integer \(N\), define the \(p\)-unit part of its factorial by
\[
 U_p(N):=\prod_{\substack{1\leq i\leq N\\p\nmid i}}i.
\]
Removing the multiples of \(p\) from \(N!\) gives the exact identity
\[
 N!=p^{\lfloor N/p\rfloor}\lfloor N/p\rfloor!\,U_p(N).       \tag{2}
\]

Fix \(r>0\), write \(q=p^r\), and let \(R\) be the set of least positive representatives of the units modulo \(q\). Thus every \(u\in R\) is prime to \(p\), and \(1\leq u<q\). For \(a\geq0\), set
\[
 B_a:=\prod_{u\in R}\left(1+\frac{aq}{u}\right).
\]
We claim that, for \(p\geq5\),
\[
 B_a\equiv1\pmod {p^{3r}}.                    \tag{3}
\]

First, every factor is \(1\) modulo \(p^r\), so \(B_a\equiv1\pmod {p^r}\). To gain two further powers, we pair a unit with its negative. If \(\bar u\) is the representative of \(-u\), then \(\bar u=q-u\). We need two reciprocal-sum observations.

First,
\[
 S:=\sum_{u\in R}\frac1{u^2}\equiv0\pmod {p^r}.              \tag{4}
\]
Indeed, multiplication by \(2\) permutes the units modulo \(q\). The chosen representative of \(2u\) is congruent to \(2u\) modulo \(q\), and both are \(p\)-adic units, so their inverse squares are congruent modulo \(p^r\). Consequently
\[
 S\equiv\sum_{u\in R}\frac1{(2u)^2}=\frac14S\pmod {p^r}.
\]
Since \(3\) is a \(p\)-adic unit for \(p\geq5\), this implies (4).

Second,
\[
 \sum_{u\in R}\frac1{u\bar u}\equiv0\pmod {p^r}.             \tag{5}
\]
For each \(u\), using \(\bar u=q-u\),
\[
 \frac1{u\bar u}+\frac1{u^2}
 =\frac{q}{u^2\bar u},
\]
which is divisible by \(p^r\). Summing and using (4) proves (5).

Now reindexing one copy of \(B_a\) by \(u\mapsto -u\) gives
\[
 B_a^2
 =\prod_{u\in R}
 \left(1+\frac{aq}{u}\right)
 \left(1+\frac{aq}{\bar u}\right).
\]
Because \(u+\bar u=q\), each paired product is
\[
 1+\frac{a(a+1)q^2}{u\bar u}.
\]
Hence, writing \(f_u=a(a+1)q^2/(u\bar u)\),
\[
 B_a^2=\prod_{u\in R}(1+f_u).
\]
Every \(f_u\) is divisible by \(p^{2r}\), while (5) shows that \(\sum f_u\) is divisible by \(p^{3r}\). Every term of degree at least two in the expansion of \(\prod(1+f_u)\) is divisible by \(p^{4r}\), hence by \(p^{3r}\). Therefore
\[
 B_a^2\equiv1\pmod {p^{3r}}.
\]
We already know \(B_a\equiv1\pmod p\), so \(B_a+1\equiv2\pmod p\) is a unit. Dividing
\(B_a^2-1=(B_a-1)(B_a+1)\) by this unit proves (3).

The numbers in the interval \(aq+1,\ldots,(a+1)q\) which are not divisible by \(p\) are exactly \(aq+u\), \(u\in R\). Therefore
\[
 U_p((a+1)q)=U_p(aq)\prod_{u\in R}(u+aq)
 =U_p(aq)U_p(q)B_a.
\]
Using (3) and induction on \(a\),
\[
 U_p(aq)\equiv U_p(q)^a\pmod {p^{3r}}.          \tag{6}
\]
More generally, if \(q\mid t\), say \(t=aq\), then (6), applied to \(a\) and \(ma\), yields
\[
 \frac{U_p(mt)}{U_p(t)^m}\equiv1\pmod {p^{3r}},               \tag{7}
\]
because all the quantities being divided by are \(p\)-adic units.

Apply the factorial decomposition (2) to the numerator and denominator of \(C_m(pk)/C_m(k)\). All powers of \(p\) and all smaller factorials cancel, leaving the exact identity
\[
 \frac{C_m(pk)}{C_m(k)}
 =\frac{U_p(mpk)}{U_p(pk)^m}.                  \tag{8}
\]
If \(p^r\mid pk\), equations (7) and (8) show
\[
 \frac{C_m(pk)}{C_m(k)}\equiv1\pmod {p^{3r}}.
\]
Multiplication by \(C_m(k)\) proves (1).

We shall also use the weaker version valid for every prime \(p\),
\[
 v_p(C_m(pk)-C_m(k))\geq r                    \tag{9}
\]
when \(p^r\mid pk\). It follows by the same proof, using only the immediate congruence \(B_a\equiv1\pmod {p^r}\). Notice also from (8) that
\[
 v_p(C_m(pk))=v_p(C_m(k)).                     \tag{10}
\]

## 2. Formal exponentials and integrality

For a power series \(f\in\mathbb Q[[x]]\) with zero constant term, write
\[
 \mathcal E(f):=\sum_{j\geq0}\frac{f^j}{j!}.
\]
For every fixed coefficient this is a finite sum. Formal differentiation gives
\[
 (\mathcal E(f))'=f'\mathcal E(f),\qquad \mathcal E(f)(0)=1. \tag{11}
\]
These two conditions determine the series uniquely, coefficient by coefficient. It follows that
\[
 \mathcal E(f+g)=\mathcal E(f)\mathcal E(g),
 \quad \mathcal E(Nf)=\mathcal E(f)^N,
 \quad \mathcal E(f(x^q))=\mathcal E(f)(x^q).                \tag{12}
\]

We need the following integrality criterion.

**Integrality criterion.** Suppose \(f(0)=0\) and, for every prime \(p\), every coefficient of
\[
 pf(x)-f(x^p)                                                   \tag{13}
\]
has \(p\)-adic valuation at least \(1\). Then all coefficients of \(\mathcal E(f)\) are integers.

Here is a proof. Let \(A=\mathcal E(f)\). From (12),
\[
 A(x)^p=A(x^p)\,\mathcal E\bigl(pf(x)-f(x^p)\bigr).           \tag{14}
\]
If all coefficients of a series \(h\) are divisible by \(p\), then all nonconstant coefficients of \(\mathcal E(h)-1\) are divisible by \(p\): in the term \(h^j/j!\), the valuation is at least
\(j-v_p(j!)\geq1\) for \(j\geq1\). Thus (14) gives
\[
 A(x)^p\equiv A(x^p)\pmod p.                                  \tag{15}
\]

We prove integrality of the coefficient \(a_N=[x^N]A\) by induction on \(N\). The constant coefficient is \(1\). Assume all earlier coefficients are integers, and form an integral series \(g\in\mathbb Z[[x]]\) whose coefficients below degree \(N\) agree with those of \(A\), and whose coefficient in degree \(N\) is zero. In characteristic \(p\), Frobenius gives
\[
 g(x)^p\equiv g(x^p)\pmod p.
\]
The coefficients of \(A(x^p)\) through degree \(N\) are \(p\)-integral by the induction hypothesis, and its degree-\(N\) coefficient agrees with that of \(g(x^p)\). Comparing (15) with the Frobenius congruence therefore shows
\[
 [x^N](A^p-g^p)\equiv0\pmod p.                               \tag{16}
\]
Since \(A\) and \(g\) have constant coefficient \(1\) and agree below degree \(N\), factorization of \(A^p-g^p\) gives
\[
 [x^N](A^p-g^p)=p([x^N]A-[x^N]g)=p a_N.
\]
Equation (16), interpreted in \(\mathbb Q_p\), says \(v_p(pa_N)\geq1\), hence \(v_p(a_N)\geq0\). This holds for every prime \(p\). A rational number which has nonnegative valuation at every prime has denominator \(1\), so \(a_N\in\mathbb Z\). This proves the criterion.

For parameters \(m,s,n\geq0\), define
\[
 L_{m,s,n}(x):=n\sum_{k\geq1}C_m(sk)\frac{x^k}{k}.             \tag{17}
\]
We verify (13) for this series. If \(p\nmid k\), the degree-\(k\) coefficient of
\(pL_{m,s,n}(x)-L_{m,s,n}(x^p)\) is
\(pnC_m(sk)/k\), which is divisible by \(p\). If \(k=pj\), with \(j>0\), it is
\[
 \frac{n(C_m(psj)-C_m(sj))}{j}.
\]
Taking \(r=v_p(j)+1\), we have \(p^r\mid psj\), and (9) says that the numerator difference has valuation at least \(v_p(j)+1\); division by \(j\) leaves valuation at least \(1\). The constant coefficient is zero. Hence the integrality criterion applies:
\[
 \mathcal E(L_{m,s,n})\in\mathbb Z[[x]].                       \tag{18}
\]
In particular,
\[
 A_m(x)^n=\mathcal E(L_{m,1,n}(x))                             \tag{19}
\]
has integral coefficients. This proves the integrality assertion in the conjecture.

We record two consequences used below. First, if all coefficients of \(f-g\) are divisible by \(p^K\), where \(K\geq1\), and \(\mathcal E(g)\) is \(p\)-integral, then
\[
 \mathcal E(f)-\mathcal E(g)
 =\mathcal E(g)(\mathcal E(f-g)-1)

the coefficientwise congruence
\mathcal E(f)\equiv\mathcal E(g)\pmod {p^K}.                  \tag{20}
Indeed, the term \((f-g)^j/j!\) has valuation at least
\(jK-v_p(j!)\geq K\).

Second, differentiating (19) gives the familiar coefficient recursion. If
\(a_k=[x^k]\mathcal E(L_{m,1,n})\), then
\[
 k a_k=\sum_{j=1}^k nC_m(j)a_{k-j},\qquad a_0=1.              \tag{21}
\]
Because the \(a_k\) are integers, the right side is divisible by \(k\). Thus the natural-number recursion obtained by dividing that sum by \(k\) produces exactly these coefficients. In particular, the recursively defined integer \(b_m(n)\) is indeed
\([x^n]A_m(x)^n\).

## 3. A valuation and carry estimate

For the main congruence when \(m\geq2\), we require control of individual terms in an exponential expansion.

Legendre's formula gives, for all sufficiently large \(b\),
\[
 v_p(C_m(j))
 =\sum_{e=1}^{b-1}
 \left(\left\lfloor\frac{mj}{p^e}\right\rfloor
       -m\left\lfloor\frac j{p^e}\right\rfloor\right)
 =\sum_{e=1}^{b-1}
 \left\lfloor\frac{m(j\bmod p^e)}{p^e}\right\rfloor.         \tag{22}
\]
The last equality follows on writing
\(j=p^e\lfloor j/p^e\rfloor+(j\bmod p^e)\). In particular, every partial sum of the nonnegative terms on the right is a lower bound for \(v_p(C_m(j))\).

We now establish the carry estimate. Let \(I\) be a finite set, let \(a_i>0\) for \(i\in I\), and suppose
\[
 p^r\mid\sum_{i\in I}a_i.
\]
Assume
\[
 s\leq v_p(a_i)<r\quad(i\in I),
 \qquad \min_i v_p(a_i)=s,
 \qquad m\geq2.
\]
Then
\[
 3(r-s)+v_p(|I|!)
 \leq\sum_{i\in I}\bigl(r-v_p(a_i)+v_p(C_m(a_i))\bigr).      \tag{23}
\]

To prove this, for \(s<e\leq r\) define
\[
 W_e:=\sum_{i\in I}
 \left(\mathbf1_{v_p(a_i)<e}
 +\left\lfloor\frac{m(a_i\bmod p^e)}{p^e}\right\rfloor\right).
\]
The residues \(a_i\bmod p^e\) have a positive sum divisible by \(p^e\): divisibility follows from \(p^e\mid\sum a_i\), and positivity follows because an index attaining valuation \(s<e\) has nonzero residue. Hence their sum is at least \(p^e\). Moreover, for every nonzero residue \(c<p^e\),
\[
 mc<p^e\left(1+\left\lfloor\frac{mc}{p^e}\right\rfloor\right).
\]
Summing this strict inequality over the nonzero residues gives
\[
 mp^e\leq m\sum_i(a_i\bmod p^e)<p^eW_e.
\]
Since \(m\geq2\) and \(W_e\) is an integer, \(W_e\geq3\).

At \(e=r\), every \(v_p(a_i)<r\), so the indicator terms also show \(W_r\geq |I|\). For \(p\geq5\), Legendre's bound
\((p-1)v_p(k!)<k\) for \(k>0\) implies
\[
 v_p(k!)+3\leq\max(k,3).                                      \tag{24}
\]
Thus \(W_r\geq v_p(|I|!)+3\), while every other \(W_e\geq3\). Consequently
\[
 \sum_{e=s+1}^r W_e\geq3(r-s)+v_p(|I|!).                     \tag{25}
\]
On the other hand, for each fixed \(i\), summing the indicator over
\(e=s+1,\ldots,r\) gives \(r-v_p(a_i)\), and (22) bounds the sum of the floor terms by \(v_p(C_m(a_i))\). This turns (25) into (23).

## 4. The low-index exponential comparison

Fix \(p\geq5\), \(r\geq1\), and define two zero-constant-term series
\[
 F_{\rm low}(x)=
 \sum_{p^r\nmid j}\frac{np^r C_m(j)}j x^j,
\]
\[
 G_{\rm low}(x)=
 \sum_{\substack{p^r\nmid j\\p\mid j}}
 \frac{np^r C_m(j/p)}j x^j.                                  \tag{26}
\]
For \(p^r\nmid j\), put
\[
 w(j):=r-v_p(j)+v_p(C_m(j)).
\]
The degree-\(j\) coefficients of both series have valuation at least \(w(j)\). For \(G_{\rm low}\), this uses (10), and when \(p\nmid j\) its coefficient is zero. More importantly, (1) gives
\[
 v_p\bigl([x^j](F_{\rm low}-G_{\rm low})\bigr)
 \geq w(j)+3v_p(j).                                           \tag{27}
\]
Indeed, if \(p\mid j\), apply (1) to \(C_m(j)-C_m(j/p)\) with exponent \(v_p(j)\), and include the factor \(np^r/j\). If \(p\nmid j\), then \(G_{\rm low}\) has zero coefficient, and (27) reduces to the ordinary bound for \(F_{\rm low}\).

We claim that if \(m\geq2\) and \(p^r\mid M\), then
\[
 [x^M]\mathcal E(F_{\rm low})
 \equiv[x^M]\mathcal E(G_{\rm low})\pmod {p^{3r}}.            \tag{28}
\]
Consider the contribution from the \(k\)-th exponential term. Its difference is
\[
 \frac1{k!}[x^M](F_{\rm low}^k-G_{\rm low}^k).
\]
Expand it over ordered \(k\)-tuples \((a_1,\ldots,a_k)\) of nonnegative integers with sum \(M\). If some \(a_i\) is divisible by \(p^r\), the corresponding coefficient in both low series is zero, so that tuple contributes zero. Otherwise all \(a_i>0\) and \(v_p(a_i)<r\). Let
\(s=\min_i v_p(a_i)\). A telescoping expansion of the difference of the two products, together with the individual estimates and (27), shows that its valuation is at least
\[
 \sum_i w(a_i)+3s.
\]
By (23), this is at least
\[
 3(r-s)+v_p(k!)+3s=3r+v_p(k!).
\]
After division by \(k!\), the valuation is at least \(3r\). Every tuple, hence every \(k\)-th exponential term and finally their finite sum in degree \(M\), has this valuation. This proves (28).

We shall also need that \(\mathcal E(F_{\rm low})\) is \(p\)-integral. In fact, if \(p^r\nmid j\), then \(v_p(j)<r\), and integrality of \(C_m(j)\) gives
\[
 v_p\left(\frac{np^rC_m(j)}j\right)\geq r-v_p(j)\geq1.
\]
Thus every coefficient of \(F_{\rm low}\) is divisible by \(p\), and the same factorial estimate used after (13) shows that its exponential is \(p\)-integral.

## 5. The diagonal congruence for \(m\geq2\)

Write \(t=r-1\), so the desired exponent is \(3(t+1)\), and put
\[
 q=p^{t+1}.
\]
The high-index logarithms satisfy
\[
 L_{m,q,n}\equiv L_{m,p^t,n}\pmod {p^{3(t+1)}}                \tag{29}
\]
coefficientwise. Indeed, in positive degree \(j\) their difference is
\[
 \frac n j\bigl(C_m(p^{t+1}j)-C_m(p^tj)\bigr).
\]
Apply (1) with \(n\) there replaced by \(p^tj\) and with exponent
\(t+1+v_p(j)\). Since \(C_m(p^tj)\) is integral, the resulting valuation, after division by \(j\), is at least \(3(t+1)\). By (18), \(\mathcal E(L_{m,p^t,n})\) is \(p\)-integral, so (20) turns (29) into
\[
 \mathcal E(L_{m,q,n})
 \equiv\mathcal E(L_{m,p^t,n})
 \pmod {p^{3(t+1)}}                                           \tag{30}
\]
coefficientwise.

The point of the low series is supplied by the following exact decompositions, obtained simply by separating indices divisible by \(q\):
\[
 L_{m,1,nq}(x)=L_{m,q,n}(x^q)+F_{\rm low}(x),                 \tag{31}
\]
where \(F_{\rm low}\) is (26) with \(r=t+1\), and
\[
 L_{m,1,np^t}(x^p)=L_{m,p^t,n}(x^q)+G_{\rm low}(x).           \tag{32}
\]
For (31), the term with index \(j=qk\) becomes
\(nC_m(qk)x^{qk}/k\), exactly the \(k\)-th term of
\(L_{m,q,n}(x^q)\); all other indices form \(F_{\rm low}\).
For (32), an exponent in the left side is first required to be divisible by \(p\). Those divisible by \(q\) form the high series, and those divisible by \(p\) but not by \(q\) form \(G_{\rm low}\).

Exponentiating (31) and (32), set
\[
 F=\mathcal E(L_{m,q,n})(x^q),\quad
 G=\mathcal E(L_{m,p^t,n})(x^q),
\]
\[
 U=\mathcal E(F_{\rm low}),\quad
 W=\mathcal E(G_{\rm low}).
\]
Then
\[
 \mathcal E(L_{m,1,nq})=FU,
 \qquad
 \mathcal E(L_{m,1,np^t})(x^p)=GW.                            \tag{33}
\]
By (30), \(F-G\) is coefficientwise divisible by \(p^{3(t+1)}\), while \(U\) is \(p\)-integral. Hence every coefficient of \((F-G)U\) is divisible by that power.

For \(G(U-W)\), consider its coefficient in degree \(nq\). The series \(G\) is supported only in degrees divisible by \(q\). Thus, in each convolution term, either the degree taken from \(G\) is not divisible by \(q\), in which case it is zero, or it is divisible by \(q\), in which case the complementary degree is also divisible by \(q\). For that complementary degree, (28) says that the coefficient of \(U-W\) is divisible by \(p^{3(t+1)}\). Since \(G\) is \(p\)-integral by (18), the whole degree-\(nq\) coefficient of \(G(U-W)\) is divisible by \(p^{3(t+1)}\).

Using
\[
 FU-GW=(F-G)U+G(U-W),
\]
we conclude from (33) that
\[
 [x^{nq}]\mathcal E(L_{m,1,nq})
 \equiv [x^{nq}]\mathcal E(L_{m,1,np^t})(x^p)
 \pmod {p^{3(t+1)}}.
\]
Because \(nq=p(np^t)\), the second coefficient is
\([x^{np^t}]\mathcal E(L_{m,1,np^t})\). Therefore, for every \(m\geq2\),
\[
 [x^{np^{t+1}}]A_m(x)^{np^{t+1}}
 \equiv[x^{np^t}]A_m(x)^{np^t}
 \pmod {p^{3(t+1)}}.                                         \tag{34}
\]

## 6. The case \(m=1\)

Here \(C_1(k)=1\), so
\[
 A_1(x)=\exp\left(\sum_{k\geq1}\frac{x^k}{k}\right)
 =\frac1{1-x}.
\]
Consequently, for \(N>0\),
\[
 b_1(N)=[x^N](1-x)^{-N}
 =\binom{2N-1}{N}
 =\frac12\binom{2N}{N}
 =\frac12C_2(N).                                               \tag{35}
\]
Apply (1) with \(m=2\), \(n=np^t\), and \(r=t+1\). Its divisibility hypothesis holds because
\(p^{t+1}\mid p(np^t)\). Since \(C_2(np^t)\) is integral,
\[
 C_2(np^{t+1})-C_2(np^t)

equiv0\pmod {p^{3(t+1)}}.
\]
As \(p\geq5\), division by \(2\) does not change the \(p\)-adic valuation. Equation (35) therefore gives (34) also when \(m=1\).

Finally take \(t=r-1\). Equations (19), (21), (34), and the \(m=1\) argument show that the associated numbers are integers and that
\[
 b_m(np^r)\equiv b_m(np^{r-1})\pmod {p^{3r}}
\]
for every positive \(m,n,r\) and every prime \(p\geq5\), as required.
